elements.element: Customer may assign to an affiliate without consent.
elements.evidence: Revised Section 20(d) permits assignment only "to a successor to its business or assets on written notice"; there is no affiliate carve-out, so an affiliate transfer still falls under "any other assignment requires the written consent of the other party."

elements.element: Customer may assign to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all assets without consent.
elements.evidence: "Either party may assign this Agreement to a successor to its business or assets on written notice to the other party" — no consent required for a successor-to-business-or-assets transfer; Section 3(c) is conformed ("except as permitted by Section 20(d)") so it no longer bars this.

elements.element: Vendor may not assign without Customer's consent.
elements.evidence: The new 20(d) is mutual: Vendor (as "either party") may assign to a successor on notice alone, without Customer's consent.

elements.element: Customer's consent to Vendor assignment is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: "any other assignment requires the written consent of the other party, which shall not be unreasonably withheld" — applies to a Vendor assignment outside the successor carve-out.

elements.element: Vendor may never assign to a Customer competitor.
elements.evidence: No competitor prohibition appears in the rendered 20(d) or 3(c); nothing restricts the identity of a Vendor successor assignee.

elements.element: Customer's change of control gives Vendor no termination right.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: neither cited paragraph (20(d), 3(c)) nor, per the review of Section 17, contains any change-of-control termination or re-pricing right, and the redline introduces none.

elements.element: Both parties may assign to a successor.
elements.evidence: "Either party may assign this Agreement to a successor to its business or assets" — expressly mutual; conforming edit to 3(c) removes the contradictory absolute bar.

elements.element: A successor assignment requires written notice.
elements.evidence: "...to a successor to its business or assets on written notice to the other party."

"any other assignment requires the written consent of the other party"; no retained no-consent exception (no affiliate or other carve-out) survives — 3(c) now defers only to 20(d) and keeps the separate transfer/lease/export/sublicence consent requirement.

elements.element: Consent to other assignments is not to be unreasonably withheld.

reasons: Fallback checklist is complete on the operative text: mutual successor assignment on written notice, consent required for all other assignments, and an express reasonableness standard.

Preferred level is not reached — no affiliate carve-out for Customer, Vendor retains a no-consent successor assignment right, and there is no bar on assignment to a Customer competitor. That is acceptable because the rule permits landing at the fallback, but the drafter should note in the rationale that the position sits at the fallback rather than the preferred.

Minimality holds: only Section 20(d) is rewritten (the clause that failed every fallback element) and Section 3(c) receives a narrow conforming cross-reference ("except as permitted by Section 20(d)") while retaining the transfer, lease, export and sublicence consent restrictions verbatim. No survival tail, expense language, notice period or other extra requirement is added.

Intent preserved: the Section 3(c) edit is a cross-reference to an existing, valid section and prevents a contradictory retained sentence (an absolute bar on assignment sitting alongside the new successor right); no defined term is orphaned and no dangling reference is created.
No change-of-control cure was needed, and none was attempted — correctly scoped.
